title: AI on arXiv this week — 16 October 2026
global_caveat: arXiv has no official trending chart. This is an inferred editorial selection, not a popularity leaderboard; citation and readership signals are especially limited for papers submitted this week.

sections.title: Training Language Models to Fail Gracefully
sections.abstract: The authors introduce GracefulRL, an RL method intended to preserve task-solving ability while teaching language models to fall back safely when acting is unreliable, using outcome-level rewards without explicit fallback labels or a test-time verifier.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors say GracefulRL reshapes optimization so fallback behavior can emerge from outcome-level rewards; their abstract reports results across multiple tasks and model scales.
sections.unique_caveat: The reported evidence is task- and scale-bound; it does not establish safety in live settings where an erroneous action has irreversible consequences.

sections.title: The Wealth of Agents: Scaling Agentic AI Across Developers
sections.abstract: The authors study multi-developer agentic systems that combine independently developed specialist agents; on GAIA, they report that agents individually at or below 35% accuracy reach 70% when combined.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors make a preliminary case for collaborative, multi-developer systems as a scaling axis, supported by empirical comparisons and theoretical models.
sections.unique_caveat: The paper reports that coordination overhead can outweigh the benefits on a narrow web-search task (SealQA); its headline GAIA result should not be assumed to generalize across task mixes.

sections.title: ActiveEvidence: Decision-Focused Evidence Graphs with Verifiable Acquisition Gaps
sections.abstract: ActiveEvidence uses counterfactual evidence interaction graphs and gap-directed refinement to decide which paid visual evidence to acquire and when to stop, with certificates tied to a frozen execution trace.
sections.claimed_contribution: On 640 cases, the authors report task score 0.842 and 0.992 action agreement in dense replay, while evaluating 19.6 rather than 191.4 expensive interaction terms per decision.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors explicitly say the certificate establishes policy-consistent optimality under the pinned learned score, not semantic correctness; semantic quality is evaluated separately.

sections.title: Co-Evolving Acting and Forecasting for Language Agents
sections.abstract: CoPE trains a language-agent policy to forecast future actions from earlier histories as well as act from the current one, reusing successful trajectories as multi-step supervision without adding inference-time models.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors report stronger aggregate results than GRPO and predictive-target baselines on simulated environments, improvements on two application benchmarks, and up to 1.9×/2.0× sample efficiency over ECHO/GRPO on ScienceWorld.
sections.unique_caveat: The paper reports a negative result on the Airline domain of τ²-bench, and the strongest sample-efficiency result is benchmark-specific.

sections.title: One Task, Many Interfaces: Simple Cross-Interface Consistency Training Improves LLM Agent Robustness
sections.abstract: The authors propose Cross-Interface Policy Regularization (CIPR), which trains an agent to produce consistent action distributions across two semantically equivalent but differently encoded interfaces.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors report that held-out interface perturbations reduce post-trained agent accuracy by nearly 25%, while CIPR recovers 10.5% without reducing accuracy on the unchanged interface.
sections.unique_caveat: The abstract's quantitative example is for agentic function calling; it does not establish robustness across all real-world interfaces or tasks.

sections.title: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting
sections.abstract: The authors find that agentic research searches can plateau as agents accumulate history, and report that periodically resetting search state while retaining the best candidate can improve results under a fixed budget.
sections.claimed_contribution: Across four tasks in heuristic programming, kernel optimization, and model training, the authors report gains of up to 15% over parallel agents and 39% over a single agent.
sections.unique_caveat: The evidence covers four specified tasks; it does not show that forgetting improves all forms of open-ended discovery or that no useful search state is lost.
